title: Courts and parliament

match.reason: None of the three bank points teaches that parliament is supreme and can codify or abrogate common law while courts influence it through their decisions and comments; the bill of rights point is related but covers a different debate.

draft.title: Courts and parliament
card: Supremacy
Parliament is supreme in law-making. If a statute and common law conflict, the statute prevails, within the limits of the Constitution.
Codify
parliament can collect common law rules into an Act. The rules then become statute law.
Abrogate
parliament can override a common law rule by passing an Act that cancels or changes it.
Court influence
courts can still influence parliament. A decision may expose a gap in the law, and judges may comment that reform is needed. Parliament may then act, but it does not have to.
draft.remember: Parliament can codify or abrogate common law, and court decisions and comments can prompt it to act.

a.q: Parliament passes an Act that cancels a common law rule made in an earlier case. What is this called?
opts: Abrogation
Codification
Distinguishing
Persuasion
a.why: Abrogating means overriding or cancelling common law by statute. Codification is the tempting wrong answer: it puts common law rules into an Act, rather than cancelling them.
a.clue: Think of the Act removing the rule, not collecting it.

b.q: A judge in Ballarat says a gap in the law caused an unfair result and suggests parliament should consider reform. What is the effect of this comment?
opts: It may prompt parliament to act, but it need not
It forces parliament to pass a new Act
It changes the law at once for all courts
It has no effect, as courts cannot influence parliament
b.why: Judges' comments can draw attention to problems and may lead parliament to reform the law. Parliament is supreme, so it is free to decide whether to act. The comment does not bind parliament or change the law itself.
b.clue: Who has the final say in law-making?

b.best: It may prompt parliament to act, but it need not

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('may... need not'). Every distractor is an absolute claim ('no effect', 'forces', 'at once for all courts'), so a test-wise student could pick the answer without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The card and both answers are accurate. In question b, the right option is the only qualified choice among absolute distractors, which partly gives the answer away.
